summary: Describes the Russian federal standard algorithms for encryption, decryption and message authentication codes, GOST 28147-89. It was written as information for developers and users of Russian cryptography in Internet applications. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: It explains a secret-code method used in Russia for locking and unlocking messages and checking nobody changed them.

questions: how many rounds does gost 28147-89 use
subtitle: How the Russian GOST 28147-89 block cipher encrypts, decrypts and authenticates data, written down for Internet developers.

tldr.problem: Russian cryptography was starting to be used in Internet applications, but developers and users had no description of the GOST 28147-89 standard in the RFC series.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC describes a 64-bit block cipher with a 256-bit key and 32 rounds, and its four working modes: electronic codebook, counter, cipher feedback and MAC generation.
tldr.outcome: It is an Informational document for information only, not a standard, and it has been updated by RFC 8891. It leaves the S-box tables open.

today: RFC 5830 is an Informational document and has been updated by RFC 8891. It is published for information and is not an Internet Standards Track specification.

sections.title: What GOST 28147-89 Is
sections.content:
GOST 28147-89 is described as the unified cryptographic transformation algorithm for information processing systems of different purposes. It defines rules for encryption and decryption and rules for generating a message authentication code (MAC). It is meant for hardware or software implementation.

The RFC says the standard defines the encryption model and MAC generation for messages sent over insecure public telecommunication channels, and that it is obligatory to use in the Russian Federation in all data processing systems providing public services. This RFC was written as a source of information, not as an Internet standard.
sections.plainLanguage: It is a rulebook for locking and unlocking messages, and for putting a seal on them so you can tell if someone changed them.

sections.title: The Cryptographic Model
sections.content:
The model is described as a set of registers and adders. A 256-bit key store holds eight 32-bit registers, X0 to X7. Four 32-bit registers, N1 to N4, hold working data, and two more, N5 and N6, hold the constants C1 and C2. There are adders for modulo 2^32, modulo 2 and modulo 2^32-1, and a register that does a cyclic shift of 11 steps.

The substitution box (S-box) splits a 32-bit input into eight 4-bit pieces. Each piece goes through its own table of 16 lines. The standard itself does not define any S-boxes; the RFC notes that some are defined in RFC 4357. Keys and S-box tables are secret elements provided through an established procedure. The model has four working modes: ECB, counter (CNT), cipher feedback (CFB) and MAC generation. The CBC mode in RFC 4357 is not part of the standard.
sections.plainLanguage: Picture a machine with a row of little boxes holding numbers. The secret key lives in eight of them, and a scrambling table mixes the numbers each turn.

sections.title: Encrypting Blocks in Electronic Codebook Mode
sections.content:
In electronic codebook (ECB) mode the plain text is split into 64-bit blocks. Each block is loaded into N1 and N2 and put through 32 rounds. In a round, N1 is added modulo 2^32 to one key register, the result goes through the S-box, is shifted left by 11 and is combined bitwise modulo 2 with N2. The result goes into N1 and the old N1 into N2.

The key registers are used in a fixed order: X0 to X7 three times, then X7 back to X0 for rounds 25 to 32. Decryption uses the same algorithm with the key order X0 to X7 once, then X7 to X0 three times. The RFC writes the encryption of a block as A, and the other modes build on it.
sections.plainLanguage: The message is cut into small chunks. Each chunk is scrambled 32 times with the secret key, and unscrambling uses the key in a different order.

sections.title: Counter and Cipher Feedback Modes
sections.content:
In counter mode the text is combined bitwise modulo 2 with a running key made 64 bits at a time. A 64-bit initialisation vector S is first encrypted in ECB mode. The two halves are then adjusted with the constants (C2 added modulo 2^32 to one half, C1 added modulo 2^32-1 to the other), and the result is encrypted again to give each block of the running key. The constants are listed in Appendix A. The initialisation vector and the encrypted blocks are what gets transmitted.

In cipher feedback mode the first running key block is the encryption of S. After that, each encrypted block is fed back into the registers to produce the next running key block. In both modes the last block can be shorter than 64 bits, and the unused part of the running key is discarded. Decryption repeats the key stream generation and combines it with the ciphertext in the same way.
sections.plainLanguage: Instead of scrambling the message directly, the machine makes a long secret stream of noise and mixes it into your message. The receiver makes the same noise and mixes it again to get the message back.

sections.title: Message Authentication Code Generation
sections.content:
To protect a message of M 64-bit blocks (with M at least 2) from falsification, an additional l-bit block, the MAC, is generated. The process is the same for all the encryption modes. The first block is run through the first 16 rounds of the ECB algorithm, using the same key as for the encryption. The result is combined bitwise modulo 2 with the next block and run through 16 rounds again, and so on to the last block, which is padded with zeros if needed.

The MAC is a chosen l-bit part of the final result and is attached to the end of the encrypted data. The receiver decrypts, recomputes the MAC and compares. If the two differ, the plain text is considered false. The RFC says the bit length l depends on the actual cryptographic requirements, and the chance of imposing false data is 2^-l. The first blocks may carry unencrypted service information such as an address section or a time mark.
sections.plainLanguage: The machine makes a short stamp from the whole message. If even one letter changes on the way, the stamp the receiver makes will not match.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC's whole security section is one sentence: this entire document is about security considerations. It adds no separate analysis of the strength of the cipher.

Where the text does bear on security, it says that keys and S-box tables are secret elements. It also says that the standard does not define S-boxes, so choosing them is left to other documents such as RFC 4357.
sections.plainLanguage: The authors say the whole document is about keeping secrets safe, so they did not add a separate warning page.
